Fluid force by horizontal stripsAt a depth x below the fluid surface, the pressure depends on depth through h(x), while the surface contributes a horizontal width w(x). This gives the ingredients for the force on a very thin strip.

plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 5.8.4
plan.contextChunk: This figure contains three panels, (a), (b), and (c), illustrating the derivation of the integral formula for fluid force on a submerged vertical surface. Panel (a): a cross-section of a fluid environment showing a blob-shaped surface submerged vertically, with the depth axis pointing downward; depth bounds a and b are marked with dashed red lines, depth h(x) is labeled from the fluid surface to the current level x, and width w(x) is shown as a horizontal segment across the surface at depth x. Panel (b): the same surface divided into n horizontal strips A1, A2, ..., An by partition points a = x0, x1, ..., x_{n-1}, b = xn along the depth axis. Panel (c): a close-up of the kth strip showing the sampling point x*_k between x_{k-1} and xk, with the strip approximated as a rectangle of width w(x*_k) and height Delta_xk, and depth h(x*_k) labeled. The figure sets up the Riemann sum F approx sum rho h(x*_k) w(x*_k) Delta_xk whose limit yields the fluid force integral F = integral from a to b of rho h(x) w(x) dx.

demo_steps.title: Start with one depth slice
demo_steps.narration: At a depth x below the fluid surface, the pressure depends on depth through h(x), while the surface contributes a horizontal width w(x). This gives the ingredients for the force on a very thin strip.

demo_steps.title: Partition the surface
demo_steps.narration: The interval from a to b is divided into n horizontal strips. Moving the selected k highlights one strip and shows the corresponding sample depth, width, and thickness in the close-up.

demo_steps.title: Refine the approximation
demo_steps.narration: Increasing n makes the strips thinner, so each curved strip is better approximated by a rectangle of area w(x*_k) Delta x_k. The displayed sum becomes a better approximation to the true fluid force.

demo_steps.title: Watch the sum become an integral
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the animated construction to see the strip contributions accumulate across the surface. In the limit as the maximum strip thickness goes to zero, the Riemann sum becomes the integral from a to b.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Each force term is pressure at a representative depth times the area of a thin horizontal strip, so summing all strips and refining the partition gives F = integral from a to b of rho h(x) w(x) dx.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a vertical textbook-style layout for the three-panel mode: panel (a) on top, panel (b) in the middle, and panel (c) at the bottom. Keep the fluid light blue, the submerged surface pale yellow with a dark irregular outline, the construction guide lines red dashed, and the width segments bright blue. In panel (b), redraw the number of horizontal partition strips according to n and highlight the selected kth strip with a translucent green overlay matching the close-up rectangle in panel (c). In animated mode, show one enlarged panel rather than three stacked panels: begin with the whole submerged surface, add partition lines, move a highlighted strip downward through k = 1 to n, and update a running sum readout whose current term is rho h(x*_k) w(x*_k) Delta x_k.

authoredContext:
Suppose that a flat surface is immersed vertically in a fluid of weight density ρ and that the submerged portion of the surface extends from x = a to x = b along an x-axis whose positive direction is down (Figure 5.8.4a). For a ≤ x ≤ b, suppose that w(x) is the width of the surface and that h(x) is the depth of the point x. Define what is meant by the fluid force F on the surface, and find a formula for computing it. The basic idea for solving this problem is to divide the surface into horizontal strips whose areas may be approximated by areas of rectangles. These area approximations, along with inequalities (4), will allow us to create a Riemann sum that approximates the total force on the surface. By taking a limit of Riemann sums we will then obtain an integral for F. To implement this idea, we divide the interval [a, b] into n subintervals by inserting the points x1, x2,...,xn−1 between a = x0 and b = xn. This has the effect of dividing the surface into n strips of area Ak,k = 1, 2,...,n (Figure 5.8.4b). It follows from (4) that the force Fk on the kth strip satisfies the inequalities ρh(xk−1)Ak ≤ Fk ≤ ρh(xk)Ak or, equivalently, h(xk−1) ≤ Fk ρAk ≤ h(xk) Since the depth function h(x) increases linearly, there must exist a point x∗ k between xk−1 and xk such that h(x∗ k ) = Fk ρAk or, equivalently, Fk = ρh(x∗ k )Ak We now approximate the area Ak of the kth strip of the surface by the area of a rectangle of width w(x∗ k ) and height _x000b_xk = xk − xk−1 (Figure 5.8.4c). It follows that Fk may be approximated as Fk = ρh(x∗ k )Ak ≈ ρh(x∗ k ) · w(x∗ k )_x000b_xk Adding these approximations yields the following Riemann sum that approximates the total

demo_steps.title: Start with one depth slice
demo_steps.narration: At a depth x below the fluid surface, the pressure depends on depth through h(x), while the surface contributes a horizontal width w(x). This gives the ingredients for the force on a very thin strip.

demo_steps.title: Partition the surface
demo_steps.narration: The interval from a to b is divided into n horizontal strips. Moving the selected k highlights one strip and shows the corresponding sample depth, width, and thickness in the close-up.

demo_steps.title: Refine the approximation
demo_steps.narration: Increasing n makes the strips thinner, so each curved strip is better approximated by a rectangle of area w(x*_k) Delta x_k. The displayed sum becomes a better approximation to the true fluid force.

demo_steps.title: Watch the sum become an integral
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the animated construction to see the strip contributions accumulate across the surface. In the limit as the maximum strip thickness goes to zero, the Riemann sum becomes the integral from a to b.

plan.keyInsight: Each force term is pressure at a representative depth times the area of a thin horizontal strip, so summing all strips and refining the partition gives F = integral from a to b of rho h(x) w(x) dx.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Use a vertical textbook-style layout for the three-panel mode: panel (a) on top, panel (b) in the middle, and panel (c) at the bottom. Keep the fluid light blue, the submerged surface pale yellow with a dark irregular outline, the construction guide lines red dashed, and the width segments bright blue. In panel (b), redraw the number of horizontal partition strips according to n and highlight the selected kth strip with a translucent green overlay matching the close-up rectangle in panel (c). In animated mode, show one enlarged panel rather than three stacked panels: begin with the whole submerged surface, add partition lines, move a highlighted strip downward through k = 1 to n, and update a running sum readout whose current term is rho h(x*_k) w(x*_k) Delta x_k.

evaluation.notes: The generated figure captures the three-panel fluid-force strip construction with correct colors, arrows, partitions, and useful controls, but the default composition is visually compressed and some labels are too small or crowded.
action_items: Increase the effective size of the SVG figure relative to the UI, or dock/collapse the controls so the default three-panel diagram more closely matches the source scale.
Enlarge and reposition the panel (b) and panel (c) labels to restore the clear textbook hierarchy and avoid crowding around A1/A2/A3 and x_k*, x_{k-1}, x_k.
Tune the yellow surface boundary so its lower-left bulge, upper arch, and right-side taper more closely match the source silhouette.
For the default static state, consider using a more source-like symbolic partition display in panel (b) rather than showing all 8 strip boundaries with equal emphasis.
